title: Autonomous AI diabetic eye exam (IDx-DR/LumineticsCore) at the point of care raised exam completion in youth from 22% to 100% in the ACCESS randomised trial
summary: ACCESS RCT (Johns Hopkins, n=164): autonomous AI eye exam completion 100% vs 22% with referral; 25 abnormal results, 64% follow-through.
account: The ACCESS trial (NCT05131451) randomised 164 young people aged 8 to 21 with type 1 or type 2 diabetes at the Johns Hopkins Pediatric Diabetes Center, Baltimore, enrolled between 24 November 2021 and 6 June 2022, to an autonomous AI diabetic eye exam at the point of care using IDx-DR/LumineticsCore (Digital Diagnostics) or to scripted referral and education. Exam completion within six months was 100% (81 of 81) in the AI arm versus 22% in the control arm; 25 AI-arm participants had an abnormal result, of whom 64% completed follow-through with an eye-care provider versus 22% of controls. Follow-up ended 6 December 2022 and the paper appeared in Nature Communications in 2024. No individual participant's diagnosis or treatment is described.
purpose: IDx-DR/LumineticsCore is built to autonomously detect more-than-mild diabetic retinopathy from fundus images at the point of care; increasing screening completion is its intended benefit.
segment: Autonomous AI screening in paediatric diabetes care
taxonomy_note: Good fit: point-of-care autonomous screening removed the referral barrier in a racially and ethnically diverse youth population. Entered as general benefit without an event because no individually documented IDx-DR case was found; the trial reports process outcomes rather than vision outcomes.

ratings.reason: General benefit without an event: trial-level process outcomes (exam completion and follow-through) with no individual diagnosis or treatment reported.

ai_role.statement: The randomised design supports a causal effect of the autonomous AI exam on screening completion and follow-through; the trial did not report whether any participant's vision outcome changed. Senior author M.D. Abramoff is an investor, director and consultant of Digital Diagnostics (disclosed); the first author and most co-authors (nine of eleven) are Johns Hopkins investigators (co-author R. Channa is at the University of Wisconsin), and the author-contribution statement says Abramoff had no access to the underlying data at any time, so the paper is not vendor-authored.

evidence.citation: Wolf RM, Channa R, Liu TYA, Zehra A, Bromberger L, Patel D, Ananthakrishnan A, Brown EA, Prichett L, Lehmann HP, Abramoff MD (2024). Autonomous artificial intelligence increases screening and follow-up for diabetic retinopathy in youth: the ACCESS randomized control trial. Nature Communications 15:421.
evidence.title: Autonomous artificial intelligence increases screening and follow-up for diabetic retinopathy in youth: the ACCESS randomized control trial
evidence.quote: Diabetic eye exam completion rate was significantly higher (100%, 95%CI: 95.5%, 100%) in the intervention group (n = 81) than the control group (n = 83) (22%, 95%CI: 14.2%, 32.4%)(p < 0.001).

produced_by: Autonomous AI camera and software located in the diabetes clinic
Immediate result at the visit with referral only for abnormal findings
must_hold: Gradable images obtainable in the clinic
